### Goal: Exploring the notion of chance and how it applies to significance measures, and understanding the role of the assumptions made by specific tests (e.g. the t-test) using simulations based on known distributions such as rnorm() and dbinom() and applying do real world data from DuckDB/Parquet repository.



### 1.Simulation based on rnorm, to study the performance of the “unbiased” estimator of standard deviation( n, n-1 & n-2 denominators)

```{r}

#### Setting up looping numbers ####
################################
max.sample.size <- 20
n.sim <- 10000 # number of re-samplings we are going to run for each sample size

#### Setting up matrices to save data. 

sd.n <- matrix(0, nrow = n.sim , ncol =  max.sample.size) # table of data for sd with n
sd.ori <- matrix(0, nrow = n.sim, ncol = max.sample.size) # table of data for sd with n-1
sd.n2 <- matrix(0, nrow = n.sim, ncol = max.sample.size) # table of data for sd with n-2

# sqrt(  sum((x - mean(x))^2) / (n-1)    )  

x_sd_n <-  function( data){
  n = length( data)
  sqrt(  sum((data - mean(data))^2) / n )
}

x_sd_n2 <- function( data){
  n = length( data)
  sqrt(  sum((data - mean(data))^2) / (n-2) )
}

#### perform computations in a loop ####
########################################
for (sample.size in 2:max.sample.size) {
  for (i.sim in 1:n.sim) { # resample n.sim times. In each iteration:
    samp <- rnorm( sample.size , mean = 0 , sd = 1) 
    
    # first set of sd ( n)
    sd.n [ i.sim , sample.size] <-  x_sd_n(samp)
    
    #second set of sd ( n-1)
    
    sd.ori [ i.sim , sample.size] <- sd(samp)
    
    # third set of sd ( n-2)
    
    sd.n2 [i.sim , sample.size] <- x_sd_n2(samp)
    
  }
}
```


### calculating the mean and spread of each of these three standard deviation estimates across all 𝑁 for current n


```{r}

n <- 2:max.sample.size 

#apply( X = "DATAFRAME" , MARGIN = "2 -columns /. "1 - rows" , )

sd.n_spread <- apply( sd.n[ , n] , 2, sd )

#mean and spread for sd.ori ( n-1)

sd.ori_mean <- apply(sd.ori[, n], 2, mean)
sd.ori_spread <- apply(sd.ori[, n], 2, sd )

#mean and spread for sd.n2 ( n-2)

sd.n2_mean <- apply(sd.n2[, n], 2, mean)
sd.n2_spread <- apply(sd.n2[, n], 2, sd )
```

### 2: Behavior of the t-test under the null hypothesis using numerical simulation.


```{r}

arb_mean <- 2
arb_var <- 3 ; arb_sd = sqrt(arb_var)
n1 <- 7
n2 <- 9
smpl_1 <- rnorm( n1, mean = arb_mean , sd = sqrt( arb_var))
smpl_2 <- rnorm( n2, mean = arb_mean , sd = sqrt(arb_var))

#Ho: mean of smpl_1 - smpl_2 = 0
#Ha:mean of smpl_1 - smpl_2 != 0

#mean difference of smpl_1 and smpl_2

mean.diff_smpl1_2 <- mean(smpl_1) - mean( smpl_2)

t.test( smpl_1 , smpl_2 , var.equal = TRUE) # since both sample were generated from 
#via rnorm with both mean and sd known.

p_value = t.test( smpl_1 , smpl_2 , var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
p_value

#evidence is consistent with the Ho. hypothesis as p.value (0.09553928) > 0.05

```

### resmapling functions

```{r}

rsmpl <- function( n1, n2, n.sim = 10000, mu = 2, sd = sqrt(3) ) {
  
  #### Step 1: create a matrix containing the resamplings (10,000 rows for the simulations and 12 columns for the resamplings).
  ## Step 1: the resampling matrix — n.sim rows x (n1 + n2) columns.
  simulation_matrix <- matrix( rnorm(n.sim * (n1 + n2), mean = mu, sd = sd), nrow = n.sim, ncol = n1 + n2) 
  
  
  #### Step 2: define a function that will calculate the difference between the means of sample 1 and sample 2 in our representation of the data such as:
  mean.diff <- function(x) mean(x[1:n1])-mean(x[(n1+1):(n1+n2)])
  
  # Step 3: calculate the difference in the means for all rows of your matrix. Save it in an object called #sim.diff.
  
  sim.diff <- apply(simulation_matrix, 1, mean.diff)
  
  t.test_p_values <- apply(simulation_matrix, 1, function(x) t.test(x[1:n1], x[(n1 + 1):(n1 + n2)])$p.value)
  
  
  #### Step 4: calculate the brute force p-value by taking the rank of the negative absolute value of sim.diff divided by the length of sim.diff. Save this in a vector called sim.p.rk
  
  sim.p.rk <- rank( -abs(sim.diff) ) / 10000
  #
  
  list( n1 =n1 , n2 =n2 , sim.diff = sim.diff , sim.p.rk = sim.p.rk , t.test_p_values = t.test_p_values)
}


```


### visual analysis- plots

- the distribution of differences observed in all the resamplings
- the distribution of t-test p-values obtained for the pairs of samples in each resampling
- the distribution of brute-force p-values obtained for the pairs of samples in each resampling
- a scatter plot of t-test p-values versus the differences between the means in each pair of samples drawn
- a scatter plot of brute-force p-values versus the differences between the means (in this scatterplot, each point should represent a single resampling experiment, x-axis = difference, y-axis = p-value)
- a scatter plot of t-test p-values vs brute-force p-values

## --- general plot function


```{r}
plt <-  function( mtrix ){
  par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
  # (a) distribution of differences
  hist(mtrix$sim.diff, breaks = 50, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
       main = paste0("(a) Mean differences  n1=", n1, ", n2=", n2),
       xlab = "mean(n1) - mean(n2)")
  
  
  # (b) distribution of t-test p-values
  hist(mtrix$t.test_p_values, breaks = 50, col = "grey", border = "white",
       main = "(b) t-test p-values", xlab = "p-values")
  
  # (c) distribution of brute-force p-values
  hist(mtrix$sim.diff, breaks = 50, col = "lightgreen",
       main = "(c) Brute-force p-values", xlab = "p-value")
  
  # (d) t test.p values vs mean difference
  plot(  mtrix$sim.diff,mtrix$t.test_p_values, pch = 20, cex = 0.3,
         main = "t.test.p_values vs sim_difference", xlab = "difference", ylab = "t-test P-value")
  
  # (e) brute-force p vs mean difference
  plot(mtrix$sim.diff, mtrix$sim.p.rk, pch = 20, cex = 0.3, col = rainbow(2),
       main = "brute force p-values vs sim_diff", xlab = "difference", ylab = "brute-force p")
  
  # (f) t.test_p-values vs brute-force p-values
  plot( mtrix$t.test_p_values, mtrix$sim.p.rk , pch = 20, cex = 0.1, col = rainbow(2),
        cex.main =.9,
        main = "t-test p-values VS brute-force p-values", xlab = "brute-force p", 
        ylab = "t-test p")
  
  
  
  
  par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
}
```

### 3.a. Using rnorm, to create two samples that result in an insignificant t-test p-value, but represent two very different processes 

```{r}

# sampling functions 

stdr_fx <- function( n){
  rnorm( n , mean = 0 , sd = 1)
}

non_stdr_fx <- function( n){
  ctr <- sample(c(-5, 5), n, replace = TRUE) 
  rnorm( n , mean = ctr , sd = 1)
}

```

### getting 2 distinct samples 

```{r}

samp_a <- stdr_fx( 1000)
samp_b <- non_stdr_fx(100000)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

hist(samp_a)

hist(samp_b)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### 3.b. Plots the resulting distribution of p-values obtained across multiple trials under t.tests


```{r}

tot_trials <- 100000 # number of repeated experiments
n <- 100 # sample size drawn from each process


p.values <- numeric(n) 

for (i in 1:tot_trials) { p.values[i] <- t.test(stdr_fx(n), non_stdr_fx(n))$p.value 
# select  one sample from each
}
hist(p.values, breaks = 20, main = "t-test p-values: N(0,1) vs union of N(-10,1)/N(10,1)",
     xlab = "p-value", col = "grey") 
```
# The test deals with 2 distinct sample and since it's a t.test, our goal will be to assess if sample1 and sample2 have same means or not.
Ho: mean of sample1 - mean of sample =0
Ha: mean of sample1 - mean of sample !=0
based on the samples setup, where samp_a comes from a normal distribution and samp_b from an non-normal distribution, a standard t.test where var.equal=T is performed. From the plot, the 2 samples appear to have the same mean majority of the time, judging by the p-values. this may be due to the fact that the simulation is done with such a huge sample size and several trials.


### 4.a: Suppose a diagnostic test has a known sensitivity of 0.8 (i.e., it correctly identifies a true positive 80% of the time), and you screen 𝑛=15 patients who are all, in truth, positive..

For  \(n = 15\), \(k = 10\), \(p = 0.8\):

i.  \(\binom{15}{10} = \frac{15!}{10!\,5!} = \frac{15 \cdot 14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12 \cdot 11}{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \frac{360360}{120} = 3003\) 

ii.  \(0.8^{10} \times 0.2^{5}\)

 \(P(X = 10) = 3003 \times 0.8^{10} \times 0.2^{5} = 3003 \times 0.0000344 \approx 0.1032\)



```{r}
#binomial probability formula and the combinatorics (𝑛hoose 𝑘) to obtain #the probability that exactly 10 of the #15 patients test positive.


n.patients <- 15   # n: patients screened, all truly positive
p.sens     <- 0.8  # P(one truly positive patient tests)
```

### 4.b:
```{r}

dbinom(10, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)  
```


### 4.c:
```{r}
p.atleast.pbinom <- 1 - pbinom(9, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)
p.atleast.pbinom
```

### 4.d.
```{r}

sim.q4 <- rbinom(10000, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)

# Simulated P(X >= 10): the proportion of screens with >= 10 positives.
mean(sim.q4 >= 10)
```


### 4.e. 
```{r}


q.95 <- qbinom(0.95, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)
q.95
pbinom(q.95, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)      # >= 0.95
pbinom(q.95 - 1, size = n.patients, prob = p.sens)  # <  0.95

# Therefore the smallest k whose UPPER tail is at most 0.05 is:
k.star <- q.95 + 1
k.star

```
### This values suggests that really only 80% good, then getting all 15 people positive is rare (only 3.5% chance). Getting 14 or more is not rare (16.7%).



### 5a. Part B: Applying it to real data



```{r}

library(repoquet)
library(DBI)
library(duckdb)
library(ggplot2)


config_path <- "repoquet_public_example/repository_config.R"
cfg <- load_repository_config( config_path)
temp_dir <- file.path(cfg$FormattedDBPath, "duckdb_temp")
dir.create(temp_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

con <- open_duckdb(
  FormattedDBPath = cfg$FormattedDBPath,
  DBName = cfg$DBName,
  TempDirPath = temp_dir,
  GB = cfg$DuckDB_GB,
  ReadOnly = TRUE
)

nhanes_tables<- DBI::dbListTables(con)
nhanes_tables <- sort(grep("^NHANES_" , nhanes_tables, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE))
head(nhanes_tables, 5)



nhanes_table <- nhanes_tables[32] # selecting the BMI data frame
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, paste0("DESCRIBE ", nhanes_table))

bmi <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, paste0( "SELECT * FROM ", DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, nhanes_table)))

head(bmi) # view few rows and columns

nhanes_table <- nhanes_tables[62] # selecting the DEMO data frame
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, paste0("DESCRIBE ", nhanes_table))

demo <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, paste0( "SELECT * FROM ", DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, nhanes_table)))

head(demo)

dfr_m <-merge( bmi, demo , "SEQN" ) # combing the 2 data frame by sequence number

str( dfr_m)

dfr_m$RIAGENDR <- factor(dfr_m$RIAGENDR ,
                         levels = c(1, 2),
                         labels = c("male" , "female"))
#performing t. test to compare average BMI between males and females
head(dfr_m)

```

### 5.a.Normality check via shapiro wilk test and QQ plots

```{r}

male_bmi <- dfr_m$BMXBMI[ dfr_m$RIAGENDR == "male"]
female_bmi <- dfr_m$BMXBMI[ dfr_m$RIAGENDR == "female"]

 par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm( male_bmi)

qqline(male_bmi, col="red", lwd=2)

qqnorm( female_bmi)

qqline(female_bmi, col="red", lwd=2)

 par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# hist(  male_bmi ) # appears right skewed
# hist(female_bmi) # appears right skewed
#normality via test

# shapiro.test( bmi[gender =="male"]) # fails to to n= 5000 limit
# shapiro.test( bmi[gender =="female"])

# Ho: data is normally distributed
# Ha:  data is not normally distributed

ks.test(male_bmi , "pnorm") # p-value < 2.2e-16
ks.test(female_bmi , "pnorm") #p-value < 2.2e-16

#both are normal under ks test 


```

### 5.b. boxplot of bmi ~ gender

```{r}


ggplot( dfr_m,  aes(x =BMXBMI, y = RIAGENDR , fill = RIAGENDR))+geom_boxplot()+
  labs( title = "BMI across gender",
         x = "BMI",
         y= "Gender") +
  theme_classic()

```

### 5c. Performing hypothesis testing ( sample t.test)

```{r}

#Ho: median bmi in males - median bmi in females = 0
#Ha: median bmi in males - median bmi in females != 0

#since the the QQ plots + QQline showed great deviations of the points from the #line, we assume the data is not normally distributed and used non-parametric #alternative of the t.test

wilcox.test(male_bmi , female_bmi, conf.int = TRUE, paired = FALSE, formula = "lhs") #p-value < 2.2e-16


```
### Conclusion: The results suggest evidence against  the Ho:, ( p-value < 2.2e-16). This implies that the median bmi between males and females are not the same.


### 6.Numeric column with the greatest variance and overlap between outcome groups
The family income ratio variable is used in this demo. (INDFMPIR)

a. 
```{r}

male_inc <-  dfr_m$INDFMPIR [ dfr_m$RIAGENDR == "male"]
fem_inc <- dfr_m$INDFMPIR [ dfr_m $RIAGENDR == "female"]


x.male_inc <- sample(male_inc[!is.na(male_inc)],10) # random sample: 10 male incomes
x.fem_inc <- sample(fem_inc[!is.na(fem_inc)],10) # random sample: 10 female incomes


#hypothesis test

shapiro.test( x.male_inc) 
shapiro.test( x.fem_inc)
#both sample for the normal distribution


 par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(x.male_inc)
qqline(x.male_inc, col="red", lwd=2)

qqnorm( x.fem_inc)
qqline(x.fem_inc, col="red", lwd=2)

#Ho: mean family inc. in males - mean family inc. in females = 0
#Ha: mean family inc. in males - mean family inc. in females != 0

Pval <- t.test( x.male_inc , x.fem_inc)$p.value #p-value = 0.627

#Conclusion: we fail to reject the Ho: as the p-values (0.627) is less than alpha of 0.05.
#this suggest that means are between the 2 groups do not significantly differ. 95% CI: ( #-1.100656  1.774656)


#Repeating sampling process 1000X
Pvals <- numeric() # create an empty vector
n.sims <- 1000 # perform 1000 resamplings
for ( i.sim in 1:n.sims ) { # in each iteration:

  x.male_inc <- sample(male_inc[!is.na(male_inc)],10) # random sample: 10 male incomes
  x.fem_inc <- sample(fem_inc[!is.na(fem_inc)],10) # random sample: 10 female incomes

 Pvals[i.sim] <- t.test(x.male_inc, x.fem_inc)$p.value   # <-- saves into the vector
}

hist(Pvals , main = "p.values for variable with wide variance")


```

### 6.c.power anlaysis across sample with wide variance and low variance. income data vs arm circumference + simulation
```{r}
#power analysis for sample with wide variance

t.test( male_inc , fem_inc)

delta = mean(male_inc , na.rm = T ) - mean(fem_inc , na.rm = T)
sd = ( var(male_inc, na.rm = T) + var( fem_inc, na.rm = T))/2

power.t.test(delta=delta, sd=1, sig.level=0.05, n= 10 ) # power = 0.03688681
power.t.test(delta=delta, sd=1, sig.level=0.05, n= 15 ) #  power = 0.04046267
power.t.test(delta=delta, sd=1, sig.level=0.05, n= 20 ) #  power = 0.04364232


#power analysis for sample with small variance

t.test( male_armc , fem_armc) #p-value < 2.2e-16
delta_low = mean(male_armc , na.rm = T ) - mean(fem_armc , na.rm = T)
sd_low = ( var(male_armc, na.rm = T) + var( fem_armc, na.rm = T))/2

power.t.test(delta=delta_low, sd=1, sig.level=0.05, power=0.80) #n = 27.86752

```
### based on the power analysis, about n= 2388 will be required to achieve a power of 80% in the wide variance samples
and about n= 28 for power of 80% in the least varianced sample.
